The brass chandelier in the hotel’s dining room cast trembling gold across the polished mahogany, and the clink of crystal glasses against fine china seemed to hang in the air like a held breath. At table seven, the evening wore its mask of polite opulence. Madame DeRoux, the widow in sable velvet, lifted a delicate morsel of seared scallop to her lips—only to stop. Her fingers twitched, her throat caught. A quiet panic bloomed in her eyes.

Across the room, the waiter—the tall man with the waxed gloves, name tag reading Lucien—floated toward her with an unnervingly calm smile. He hovered, hovering like a moth around a flame.

Detective Moreau leaned back in his chair, nursing his nearly untouched Burgundy. He said nothing, but his eyes, calm pools of steel, hovered over Lucien as the latter inquired, “Madam… any discomfort?”

Madame DeRoux voiced only a choked gasp before her head fell forward, crimson staining the lace of her collar. The room’s silence tightened.

Lucien the waiter knelt beside her, whispering to someone unseen—calling a phone discreetly. His face betrayed not a flicker of confusion.

As the manager emptied his flask hastily onto the tablecloth while murmuring apologies, Moreau’s gaze flicked to the waiter’s right hand—discreetly tucked behind his back—then to his left, gloved, poised near an empty bread plate. The angle wasn’t lucky; it was staged.

A forgotten paring knife glinted, half-buried beneath a damask napkin—slightly askew from where it should have lain after clearing the course. Moreau caught the glint. A clue that lay waiting, buried beneath the evening’s golden veneer.
